newsitem.title: JAPAN: Corporate Japan's 96/97 profit seen rising 10 pct.
newsitem.headline: Corporate Japan's 96/97 profit seen rising 10 pct.

text.p: Corporate Japan is firmly on the track to recovery, with expectations for a double-digit growth in profits in the last business year and growing views the upswing will continue this year, analysts said on Tuesday.

"We expect Japanese companies' average year-on-year current profit rise in 1996/97 (ended March 31) to be a little over 10 percent. And we think their current profit will continue growing this business year," said Tatsuo Matsuoka, senior analyst at Daiwa Institute of Research.
It will be the third consecutive year for Japanese firms to increase their current profits and the steady recovery trend will continue, Matsuoka said.
Current profit is pre-tax and includes gains and losses made from non-operating activities.
A weak yen helped many export-oriented companies, the car industry in particular, boost profits last year.

The dollar/yen rate averaged 112 yen to the dollar in 1996/97, about 14 percent lower than a year earlier. A weak yen makes Japanese products more competitive overseas and also boosts the yen value of sales in foreign currencies.
Hiroki Matsushita, analyst at Wako Research Institute of Economics, although acknowledging the strong recovery Japanese firms were making, presented a more cautious view.
He said it may be questionable that 1996/97 growth could be considered as a substantial improvement in corporate Japan's strength because it was heavily dependent on the the weak yen.
Japanese firms current profit rose about 12.5 percent in 1994/95 and about 20.7 percent in 1995/96, he said.

Wako Research Institute said in a report on Tuesday that Japan's major companies, which had announced their earnings for the last business year by Monday, showed an average year-on-year rise of 13.53 percent in their current profit.
The report covered 667 firms, or 86.51 percent, of the 771 companies listed on the first section of the Tokyo Stock Exchange that close books at the end of March.
The report does not include financial institutions such as banks and stock brokerages.
By the time all 771 firms have announced their earnings, the average growth in current profit is likely to shrink to about 10 percent, Wako's Matsushita said.
This is because expected poor business results of semiconductor-related firms, severely hit by weak chip prices, are expected to weigh heavily on profit growth, he said.
Both Wako and Daiwa have found that the average parent current profit rise in the manufacturing sector, including the car industry, was more than 20 percent last year.
Wako said that the 1996/97 current profit rise in the non-manufacturing sector so far was a little over two percent.

"A 112.52 percent (current profit) rise in the car sector contributed to push up the overall average in 1996/97. Car makers' enjoyed good business and their orders to other sectors rose as well," Wako's Matsushita said.
Toyota Motor Corp's 1996/97 parent current profit rose 82.1 percent from the year ago and Honda Motor Co Ltd's parent current profit more than tripled in 1996/97.
"Companies which export large parts of their output benefitted from a weak yen," Matsuoka said.
Such companies include car makers and some electronics firms, like Sony Corp, which are not heavily involved in the chip business.
Sony's 1996/97 current profit tripled from a year ago.
The non-manufacturing sector includes gas and electric power firms, which were negatively impacted by a weak yen which boosted costs to buy oil and other sources of energy.
"Property and construction firms are still suffering from the burst of bubble economy in early 1990s and this is squeezing non-manufacturing sectors' profits," Matsuoka said.
